title: Indian Economy 1950–1990
summary: After independence India chose a mixed economy and a strategy of planned development through five-year plans with the goals of growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity. This chapter covers the main policies for agriculture (land reforms, Green Revolution, subsidies), industry (Industrial Policy Resolution 1956, licensing, small-scale industry, public sector) and trade (import substitution) from 1950 to 1990, along with their achievements and shortcomings.

notes.heading: Choice of economic system and planning
notes.html:
Every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce. Broadly there are three systems:

CapitalistSocialistMixed
Market forces decide; means of production privately owned; profit motiveGovernment decides; means of production state-owned; social welfare motiveBoth the state and the market play a role; public and private sectors co-exist

Jawaharlal Nehru and other leaders preferred a mixed economy with a 'socialist pattern of society': a large public sector, with the private sector also allowed to function within a framework of planning and regulation.

The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 with the Prime Minister as its chairperson. The First Five Year Plan covered 1951–56. India went on to have twelve five-year plans (the last ending in 2017). In January 2015 the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India), a policy think tank.

A plan spells out how the resources of a nation should be put to use. It sets general goals and specific targets for a period. Long-term goals are set over about twenty years (a 'perspective plan'), and five-year plans serve as its base.

P.C. Mahalanobis is regarded as the architect of Indian planning. The Second Five Year Plan (1956–61), based on his ideas, emphasised rapid industrialisation with heavy industries in the public sector. He founded the Indian Statistical Institute (1931) and the journal Sankhya.

notes.heading: Goals of five-year plans
notes.html:
• Growth: increase in the country's capacity to produce goods and services, reflected in a steady rise in GDP. This needs more capital, better technology and more efficient services. The sectoral composition of GDP also changes with development (agriculture's share falls, industry and services rise).
  • Modernisation: adoption of new technology (e.g. new seed varieties for farmers, new machines for factories) and changes in social outlook, such as recognising that women should have the same rights as men.
  • Self-reliance: avoiding imports of goods, especially food, that could be produced domestically, so that India would not depend on foreign countries and become vulnerable to foreign interference. The first seven plans emphasised self-reliance.
  • Equity: ensuring that the benefits of growth reach the poor. Every Indian should be able to meet basic needs like food, a decent house, education and health care, and inequality of wealth should fall.

The goals can conflict: e.g. modern labour-saving technology may raise growth but reduce employment, which affects equity. Planners had to balance them.

notes.heading: Agriculture: land reforms
notes.html:
At independence the land tenure system had intermediaries (zamindars, jagirdars) who extracted rent without contributing to improvement. Productivity was low and land ownership highly unequal. Policy aimed at equity in landholding and higher productivity.

  • Abolition of intermediaries: tillers were made owners of land ('land to the tiller'), on the belief that ownership gives the incentive to invest and raise output. A large number of tenants came into direct contact with the government and were freed from exploitation by zamindars.
  • Land ceiling: fixing the maximum size of land that an individual could own; the surplus was to be redistributed to the landless. This aimed at reducing concentration of land ownership.
  • Tenancy reforms: regulating rent, giving security of tenure and the right to buy land.

Limitations: large landlords challenged the laws in courts and delayed implementation; many transferred land to relatives to escape ceilings; some zamindars retained large areas by claiming 'self-cultivation'; tenants were evicted in some places. Land reforms were most successful in Kerala and West Bengal, whose governments were committed to the policy of land to the tiller.

notes.heading: Agriculture: the Green Revolution
notes.html:
The Green Revolution refers to the large increase in production of food grains resulting from the use of high yielding variety (HYV) seeds, especially for wheat and rice, along with adequate fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation.

  • First phase (about mid-1960s to mid-1970s): HYV seeds were used mainly in the more affluent states such as Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, and benefited mainly wheat-growing regions.
  • Second phase (about mid-1970s to mid-1980s): the technology spread to a larger number of states and a wider variety of crops.

Achievements

  • India attained self-sufficiency in food grains and ended dependence on food imports (e.g. from the USA).
  • Farmers sold a good part of the increased output in the market (marketed surplus), so the prices of food grains fell relative to other goods, which benefited low-income groups who spend a large share of income on food.
  • The government could build buffer stocks for times of shortage.

Concerns and how they were handled

  • The technology might benefit only big farmers because inputs were costly. The government provided loans at low interest rates and subsidised fertilisers so that small farmers also benefited, and small farmers' yields did rise.
  • HYV crops were more prone to pest attacks; research institutes trained farmers in their proper use.
  • It widened regional disparities as benefits were concentrated in irrigated areas.

notes.heading: Agriculture: the debate over subsidies and the role of agriculture
notes.html:
Arguments for subsidiesArguments against subsidies
Needed to encourage farmers, especially small farmers, to adopt new technologyOnce the technology is profitable and widely adopted, subsidies should be phased out
Farming is risky; subsidies help poor farmers bear the riskBenefits go largely to the fertiliser industry and to better-off farmers in prosperous regions
Help keep food affordableImpose a heavy burden on the government budget and encourage wasteful use of resources

Most economists accept that subsidies were useful in the early phase but should be well-targeted.

Limitation of the period: although agriculture's share in GDP fell, the share of the workforce in agriculture stayed very high. In 1990 about two-thirds of the population still depended on agriculture, because industry and services did not absorb enough workers.

notes.heading: Industry: the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 and licensing
notes.html:
Industry provides more stable employment than agriculture, promotes modernisation and overall prosperity. Since the private sector lacked capital and the market was small, the state took the lead in industrial development, especially in heavy industry, through the public sector.

Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) 1956

It formed the basis of the Second Plan and classified industries into three categories:

  1. Schedule A: 17 industries exclusively owned by the state.
  2. Schedule B: industries in which the state would generally set up new units, but the private sector could supplement its efforts.
  3. Schedule C: the remaining industries, left to the private sector.

The private sector was kept under state control through industrial licensing: a licence was needed to start a new industry, expand output or diversify production. It was used to promote industry in backward regions (licences were easier to get for backward areas, along with tax benefits and cheaper electricity) and to ensure that production matched the plan's priorities.

Effect: the share of industry in GDP rose from about 11.8% in 1950–51 to about 24.6% in 1990–91, and the industrial base diversified well beyond cotton and jute textiles.

notes.heading: Small-scale industry
notes.html:
In 1955 the Village and Small-Scale Industries Committee (Karve Committee) noted the possibility of using small-scale industries for promoting rural development.

  • A small-scale industry was defined by the maximum investment in fixed assets of the unit. In 1950 this limit was ₹5 lakh; the limit was raised over time. Today such units come under MSMEs (micro, small and medium enterprises), now classified by both investment and turnover.
  • Why promoted: labour-intensive, so they generate more employment; they need less capital; they can be set up in rural areas, reducing regional imbalance; they promote equitable distribution of income.
  • Protection: the production of a number of products was reserved for the small-scale sector; they were given concessions such as lower excise duty and bank loans at lower interest rates, so that they could compete with big firms.

notes.heading: Trade policy: import substitution
notes.html:
The policy in the first seven plans was inward-looking, technically called import substitution: replacing imports with domestic production. For example, instead of importing vehicles, they would be produced in India.

  • Tariffs (taxes on imports) made imported goods costlier.
  • Quotas fixed the maximum quantity of goods that could be imported.

Aim: protect domestic firms from foreign competition until they became mature (the 'infant industry' argument), and save scarce foreign exchange.

Effects: domestic industries grew and diversified. However, protection continued for too long, so firms had little incentive to improve quality or cut costs. Indian goods were often of poor quality and high cost, and the export sector remained weak.

notes.heading: Shortcomings of the 1950–90 strategy
notes.html:
• Inefficient public sector: many public enterprises made losses but continued to function because closing them was difficult; some produced goods that the private sector could have produced more efficiently.
  • Licence-permit raj: licensing led to delays, corruption and red tape. Big industrialists obtained licences to prevent competitors from entering, not to start production.
  • Lack of competition due to protection from imports caused poor quality and high costs.
  • Agriculture: land reforms were implemented poorly; dependence of the workforce on agriculture remained high.
  • Fiscal problems: by the late 1980s high government spending and borrowing led to large deficits and a balance of payments problem, setting the stage for the reforms of 1991.

Achievements: self-sufficiency in food grains, a diversified industrial base with heavy industries, rise in the industrial share of GDP, and growth of the public sector in strategic areas.

mcqs.q: The Planning Commission of India was set up in:
mcqs.explanation: It was set up in March 1950 with the Prime Minister as chairperson. The First Plan began in 1951 and the IPR came in 1956.

mcqs.q: Who is regarded as the architect of Indian planning?
mcqs.explanation: Mahalanobis designed the Second Five Year Plan with its emphasis on heavy industry. Swaminathan is associated with the Green Revolution.

mcqs.q: Which goal of planning means that the benefits of growth should reach the poor?
mcqs.explanation: Equity means a fair distribution of the benefits of growth so that every Indian can meet basic needs.

mcqs.q: Under the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956, how many industries were reserved exclusively for the state in Schedule A?
mcqs.explanation: Schedule A covered 17 industries exclusively owned by the state; Schedule B was mixed and Schedule C was left to the private sector.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Land reforms were most successful in Kerala and West Bengal.
Reason (R): The governments of these states were committed to the policy of land to the tiller.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Political commitment allowed these states to implement land reforms effectively, while in other states landlords delayed and evaded them.

mcqs.q: During the first phase of the Green Revolution, HYV seeds were mainly used for:
options: Wheat in relatively prosperous states like Punjab
mcqs.explanation: The first phase (mid-1960s to mid-1970s) was limited mostly to wheat in affluent states such as Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.

mcqs.q: The portion of agricultural produce sold in the market by farmers is called:
mcqs.explanation: Marketed surplus is output sold after meeting the farmer's own needs. Buffer stock is grain held by the government.

mcqs.q:
Read the statements:
Statement 1: Import substitution aimed to protect domestic industries from foreign competition.
Statement 2: Tariffs and quotas were the main tools of import substitution.
options: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true
mcqs.explanation: Inward-looking trade policy protected domestic producers using tariffs (taxes on imports) and quotas (quantity limits).

mcqs.q: Which committee (1955) recommended the use of small-scale industries for promoting rural development?
mcqs.explanation: The Village and Small-Scale Industries Committee, known as the Karve Committee, made this recommendation in 1955.

mcqs.q: A major criticism of industrial licensing was that:
options: Big industrialists obtained licences to block new competitors rather than to produce
It reduced the role of the public sector
mcqs.explanation: Licences were sometimes obtained only to prevent rivals from entering an industry, leading to concentration and inefficiency.

mcqs.q: The share of industry in India's GDP between 1950–51 and 1990–91:
mcqs.explanation: Planned industrialisation roughly doubled the share of industry in GDP over this period.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an argument against farm subsidies?
options: They encourage small farmers to adopt new technology
They help farmers bear the risk of new technology
They keep food affordable for the poor
They mainly benefit the fertiliser industry and better-off farmers
mcqs.explanation: Critics argue that much of the subsidy goes to the fertiliser industry and prosperous farmers and burdens the government budget.

questions.q: What is meant by marketed surplus?
questions.answerHtml: Marketed surplus is the portion of agricultural produce that farmers sell in the market after keeping what they need for their own consumption.

questions.q: Why was it necessary for a developing country like India to follow self-reliance as a planning objective?
questions.answerHtml: To reduce dependence on foreign countries, especially for food, so that India's sovereignty would not be exposed to foreign interference.

questions.q: Explain the goal of 'modernisation' in Indian planning.
questions.answerHtml:
Modernisation means adopting new technology to increase the production of goods and services. Examples: farmers using new seed varieties instead of old ones, and factories using new machines.

It also includes changes in social outlook, such as recognising that women should have the same rights as men. In a traditional society women stay at home; a modern society uses their talents in the workplace, in banks, factories and schools, which makes society more civilised and prosperous.

questions.q: Why, despite the implementation of the Green Revolution, did about two-thirds of the population continue to be engaged in agriculture till 1990?
questions.answerHtml:
As a country develops, the share of agriculture in GDP and employment should both fall. In India, the share in GDP fell considerably, but the share in employment did not fall correspondingly because:

  • The industrial and service sectors did not grow fast enough to absorb the people working in agriculture.
  • Industries were largely capital-intensive (heavy industries), creating fewer jobs.
  • Lack of skills and education among rural workers limited their movement to other sectors.

Hence many people remained in agriculture, often as disguised unemployment.

questions.q: Explain the role of the Green Revolution in making India self-sufficient in food grains. Also mention any two of its limitations.
questions.answerHtml:
Role:

  • Use of HYV seeds with fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation sharply raised the yield of wheat and later rice.
  • A large part of the increased output was sold in the market (marketed surplus), so food grain prices fell relative to other goods.
  • The government procured grain to build buffer stocks, and India no longer depended on imports for food.

Limitations:

  1. Benefits were concentrated in irrigated, prosperous regions and crops (wheat), widening regional inequality.
  2. HYV crops are more prone to pest attacks and the heavy use of chemicals harmed soil and water over time.

questions.q: 'The public sector should not be allowed to continue if it is incurring losses.' Defend or refute in the context of the period 1950–90.
questions.answerHtml:
The statement is partly defended.

  • For: many public enterprises incurred continuous losses but were kept running because closing them was politically difficult. This drained government resources that could have been used for health and education. In areas such as hotels or consumer goods, the private sector could produce more efficiently.
  • Against (justification of the public sector): the public sector was set up not only for profit but to build heavy industry and infrastructure where private capital was lacking, to reduce regional imbalance, to generate employment and to keep strategic sectors under national control. Some losses arose from social obligations such as low pricing of essential goods.

Conclusion: loss-making units should be reformed or closed where they serve no social purpose, but the public sector's role in strategic and welfare areas cannot be judged by profit alone.

questions.q: Discuss the main features of the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 and the role of industrial licensing.
questions.answerHtml:
The IPR 1956 was adopted in line with the goal of a socialist pattern of society and formed the basis of the Second Five Year Plan. It classified industries into three categories:

  1. Schedule A: 17 industries to be exclusively owned and developed by the state (e.g. arms and ammunition, atomic energy, railways).
  2. Schedule B: industries in which the state would progressively set up new units, while the private sector would supplement its efforts.
  3. Schedule C: all remaining industries, left to the private sector.

Industrial licensing: the private sector was kept under state control through licences.

  • A licence was required to start a new industry, to expand output beyond the licensed capacity or to diversify production.
  • Licences were easier to obtain for setting up industries in economically backward areas; such units also received tax benefits and electricity at lower tariffs. This aimed at balanced regional development.
  • Licensing ensured that production matched national priorities and that the quantity of goods produced was consistent with the needs of the economy.

Criticism: licensing caused delays, corruption and the 'licence-permit raj', and big firms sometimes secured licences only to block competitors.

questions.q: Explain the policy of import substitution followed during 1950–90. Assess its effect on Indian industry.
questions.answerHtml:
Meaning: import substitution is an inward-looking trade strategy of producing at home the goods that were earlier imported, e.g. making vehicles in India instead of importing them.

Tools:

  • Tariffs: taxes on imports made imported goods costlier, so domestic goods became relatively cheaper.
  • Quotas: limits on the quantity of goods that could be imported.

Reasons: to protect domestic 'infant' industries from more developed foreign competitors until they could compete; to save scarce foreign exchange; and to promote self-reliance.

Positive effects:

  • Domestic industries, including automobiles, chemicals and machinery, grew and diversified.
  • Foreign exchange was saved for essential imports such as capital goods and crude oil.

Negative effects:

  • Protection continued for too long, so firms had little pressure to improve quality, adopt new technology or cut costs.
  • Consumers faced high prices and poor quality; choice was limited.
  • The export sector remained weak, contributing to the balance of payments problem that culminated in the crisis of 1991.
